Sectoral GHG Emissions & LULUCF Accounting Explorer

PRIMAP-hist v2.8 (HISTCR vs. HISTTP, AR5 GWP100) integrated with JRC NGHGI v4.0.0 (BTR1) & GCB 2025 Bookkeeping (1750–2025)

215 areas • HISTCR & HISTTP × NGHGI & Bookkeeping • 1750–2025

About this explorer

This explorer shows the greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions of 215 countries and country groups from 1750 to 2025, broken down by sector: energy, industrial processes and product use (IPPU), agriculture, waste and other. All values are CO₂ equivalents (CO₂eq): the emissions of each gas are converted into the amount of CO₂ with the same warming effect and then added up.

Forests, cropland and grassland both release and absorb carbon. The land use, land-use change and forestry (LULUCF) sector covers these fluxes. Land use and land-use change account for about a third of all the CO₂ that people have emitted so far, but estimates of it vary widely with the method used (Obermeier et al., 2025). This explorer compares two of these methods.

The national greenhouse gas inventories (NGHGIs) that governments report to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) count all emissions and removals on managed land as human-caused, regardless of what drives them. This includes the extra carbon that forests absorb because of rising atmospheric CO₂ and a changing climate, so the land sector often appears as a net sink (negative values). The scientific bookkeeping approach counts only the effects of what people do directly to the land, such as clearing forest for farmland, harvesting wood and replanting. As a result, the land sector often appears as a net source (positive values). The bookkeeping values come from the Global Carbon Budget (GCB).

Worldwide, the two methods differ by about 8.9 Gt CO₂ per year (2014–2023 average; Lamb et al., 2026). On this page, world LULUCF net emissions in 2024 are −4.4 Gt CO₂ with NGHGI and +4.6 Gt CO₂ with bookkeeping. Neither figure is wrong; they serve different purposes. Countries set their nationally determined contributions (NDCs) and net-zero targets under inventory conventions, so compare those with the HISTCR + NGHGI combination. The global pathways in IPCC reports use the bookkeeping approach for LULUCF, so the HISTTP + Bookkeeping combination is closer to them (Lamb et al., 2026).

How to use, and key terms
  1. Choose a Country / Region. Groups such as the World, the European Union and the Least Developed Countries are available too.
  2. Inventory Priority: HISTCR puts country-reported data first; HISTTP puts third-party estimates first, such as those of EDGAR or the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).
  3. LULUCF Accounting Method: switching between NGHGI and Bookkeeping changes the net totals in the cards, charts and table. The 2×2 method matrix shows all four combinations at a glance.
  4. You can also change the Time-Series Visualization Mode and the Historical Window & Snapshot Year. The cards and the table show values for the snapshot year.
GHG, CO₂eq, GWP100
Greenhouse gases include carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide. Because each gas has a different warming effect, its emissions are multiplied by its 100-year global warming potential (GWP100) to convert them into CO₂ equivalents before they are added up. The Paris Agreement reporting rules prescribe the values of the IPCC Fifth Assessment Report (AR5); this page uses AR5 GWP100.
Mt, Gt
1 Mt (megatonne) is one million tonnes and 1 Gt (gigatonne) is one billion tonnes, so 1 Gt = 1,000 Mt.
M.0.EL
Total emissions excluding LULUCF (energy + IPPU + agriculture + waste + other).
LULUCF
The land use, land-use change and forestry sector: carbon released or absorbed by forests, cropland, grassland and other land. Negative values are net removals, positive values net emissions.
Cat 0
Total emissions including LULUCF (M.0.EL + LULUCF), also called net emissions.
NGHGI
National greenhouse gas inventory: the official statistics that countries report in Biennial Transparency Reports (BTRs) under the Enhanced Transparency Framework (ETF) of the Paris Agreement. Since 2024 all countries must submit these reports, with some flexibility for countries such as the Least Developed Countries. The NGHGI values on this page come from the LULUCF Data Hub of the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre (JRC), which fills gaps in country reports and harmonizes them.
Bookkeeping
Scientific models that record land-use change like entries in a ledger and calculate the resulting carbon fluxes. This page uses the mean of the three models (BLUE, OSCAR and LUCE) in the national data of the Global Carbon Budget 2025. They count the changes that people cause directly and leave out the extra carbon that forests absorb because of rising atmospheric CO₂ or climate change.
HISTCR, HISTTP
The two priority settings of PRIMAP-hist. Complete annual national inventories exist only for Annex I countries from 1990 onwards, which account for about a third of global emissions, so third-party estimates fill the gaps (Lamb et al., 2026). HISTCR puts country-reported data first and fills gaps with third-party estimates; HISTTP puts third-party estimates first. Their difference (CR − TP) shows how much the values depend on that choice.
IPPU, M.AG
IPPU covers emissions from industrial processes such as cement, steel and chemicals and from the use of products such as refrigerants. M.AG covers agricultural emissions from livestock, fertilizers, rice cultivation and similar sources.

LULUCF values for 1750–1849 and NGHGI values before 2000 are estimates made for this page. LULUCF for 2025 repeats the 2024 value. LULUCF on this page covers CO₂ only.

Why the two LULUCF methods differ

The carbon that forests release and absorb has three kinds of causes, which measurements cannot easily tell apart (Lamb et al., 2026):

  • Direct anthropogenic effects: what people do to the land, such as clearing forest for farmland, harvesting wood and replanting
  • Indirect anthropogenic effects: how forests respond to human-caused environmental change, such as rising atmospheric CO₂, climate change and nitrogen deposition
  • Natural effects: year-to-year weather, fires, pests and other natural events

The IPCC guidelines treat all emissions and removals on managed land as human-caused, whatever the driver. This convention is called the managed land proxy. Managed land is land where people intervene to perform production, ecological or social functions; besides cropland and managed forests, it can include national parks, indigenous lands and areas under fire protection. Most Annex I countries report all of their forests as managed. Some countries, such as Australia and Canada, exclude large wildfires from their totals as natural disturbances. Bookkeeping models, by contrast, separate the human share by cause rather than by location, and count direct effects only (Lamb et al., 2026).

Adding the carbon that managed forests absorb through indirect and natural effects to the bookkeeping values closes most of the gap between the two methods (Obermeier et al., 2025). The JRC LULUCF Data Hub publishes values “translated” in this way, and this page estimates NGHGI values before 2000 by the same method. How large the gap is, and in which direction, varies from country to country.

Why totals differ from other sources

Even for the same year, global emissions totals differ by several Gt CO₂eq depending on the data used and on what is included. Averaged over 2014–2023, totals aligned with national inventories (the HISTCR + NGHGI combination on this page) are 44.4 Gt CO₂eq per year, while totals comparable with IPCC pathways are 54.5 Gt CO₂eq. About 8.9 Gt of the 10.1 Gt difference comes from the LULUCF method (Lamb et al., 2026). Other differences:

  • International aviation and shipping: not assigned to any country and not included in PRIMAP-hist (about 1.1 Gt CO₂ per year, 2014–2023 average).
  • Outside the Paris Agreement: ozone-depleting substances (ODS) regulated under the Montreal Protocol, namely CFCs and HCFCs, emitted about 1.5 Gt CO₂eq in 2022. Cement carbonation, the CO₂ that cement takes up again from the air, removes about 0.8 Gt CO₂ per year. Neither is part of national inventories or of this page.
  • Methane: national inventories tend to report lower methane emissions from coal, oil and gas production than third-party estimates. Globally, most of the difference between HISTCR and HISTTP comes from methane (Lamb et al., 2026).
  • Emission factors: third-party estimates often use global average emission factors (Tier 1), while most Annex I countries use national factors or models (Tier 2 or Tier 3). Values and trends can therefore differ by country (Lamb et al., 2026).
  • GWP values: using AR5 or AR6 GWP100 slightly changes the CO₂eq values of methane and nitrous oxide. This page uses AR5 GWP100.
  • Uncertainty: the uncertainty of net LULUCF emissions in national inventories (95% confidence interval) is about 35% for Annex I countries and about 50% for non-Annex I countries (Obermeier et al., 2025).
